html:
An Indian law of 2005 that gives every citizen the right to ask any public authority for information and to get an answer, as a rule within 30 days.

It grew from a grassroots campaign. In the 1990s, the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, a union of workers and farmers in Rajasthan co-founded by Aruna Roy, held public hearings where villagers read out official records of local spending. They found wages paid to dead people and roads that existed only on paper. The slogan "our money, our accounts" spread, several states passed their own laws, and the national act followed under the government of Manmohan Singh.

Millions of requests are filed every year, on everything from ration cards to ministers' decisions, and the law has exposed corruption and forced officials to act. It has also been dangerous: dozens of RTI activists have been killed. Critics say later amendments and unfilled commission posts have weakened it. Passed in the same year as the rural employment guarantee, it was part of a wave of rights-based laws, based on the right to free expression in the Constitution of India.
sum: An Indian law of 2005 that gives every citizen the right to ask any public authority for information and to get an answer, as a rule within 30 days.
